thread.title: Farnborough Airshow: Will Boeing, Airbus Supercycle Start To Cool Off?

author: GILLIAN RICH
title: Farnborough Airshow: Will Boeing, Airbus Supercycle Start To Cool Off?
text:
Boeing ( BA ) and Airbus ( EADSY ) are scrambling to keep up with booming demand for passenger jets as middle classes grow in India and China, and the Farnborough Airshow is expected to swell their overflowing order books even further.
X The aerospace industry's biggest event, which alternates with the Paris Air Show each year, runs July 16-22.
Prior to Farnborough, the Royal International Air Tattoo will showcase military aircraft this Friday to Sunday. Lockheed Martin ( LMT ) F-35s and F-16s will perform some aerobatics as well as Typhoon fighters, which is made by a consortium that includes Airbus. General Atomics' MQ-9B drone will also make an appearance after making its first transatlantic flight.
Boeing, Airbus Supercycle Demand for commercial jets is in a supercycle, and while the industry is overdue for a correction, Teal Group aerospace consultant Richard Aboulafia doesn't see demand slowing down anytime soon.
"When the smoke clears, we are probably going to see 300-400 real orders," he said. "Then another 400-500 semi-orders," like memorandums of understanding.
The combined 700-900 orders and commitments Aboulafia sees would be comparable with the nearly 900 Boeing and Airbus racked up at last year's Paris Air Show and up sharply from the roughly 450 that the two archrivals tallied at the prior Farnborough Airshow in 2016.
In particular, demand from low-cost airlines and Asian carriers is expected to continue soaring.
Last month, India's Jet Airways ordered 75 Boeing 737 Max jets for $8.8 billion. Also in June, Vietnam's Bamboo Airways ordered 20 787 Boeing Dreamliners worth $5.6 billion. Late last year, China Aircraft Leasing agreed to buy 50 A320neos in a deal worth $5.42 billion.
So far this year, Boeing is crushing European rival Airbus on orders. During the first six months of 2018, Boeing booked 460 orders, after cancellations, while Airbus only booked 206 net orders.
"We are in a really good place today," Randy Tinseth, Boeing's VP of marketing, told IBD last month when asked about orders at the air show.
But Airbus has a history of securing massive orders during airshows. Indeed, at the Dubai Airshow in December, Airbus clinched a $49.5 billion order from U.S. private equity fund Indigo Partners for 430 aircraft, in what is considered one of the biggest aviation deals ever.
However, this year's Farnborough Airshow will be the first major event in 33 years for Airbus without rainmaker John Leahy. The form sales chief secured aircraft orders worth more than a trillion dollars during his tenure.
 Narrow Body, Widebody Competition Aboulafia expects most of the orders at the Farnborough Airshow to be for narrow-body jets. Boeing's 737 Max and Airbus' A320neo have been especially popular with low-cost carriers and rapidly expanding airlines in Asia.
But even smaller jets make see greater prominence as Airbus and Boeing use their global marketing heft to push aircraft in the emerging category.
Airbus took a majority stake in Bombardier 's ( BDRBF ) single-aisle C Series business in October and just renamed the line the A220. On Tuesday, JetBlue ( JBLU ) announced an order for 60 A220-300s and more could come at Farnborough.
Boeing announced last week it will take a controlling stake in the commercial segment of Brazil's Embraer ( ERJ ) as it looks to counter Airbus.
Another category to watch is the widebody class. In recent months, Boeing's 787 has won orders at the expense of Airbus' A330 .
Indian carrier Vistara announced Tuesday that it has placed firm orders for six Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners . Meanwhile, United Airlines ( UAL ) is reportedly leaning toward buying 787s to replace up to 50 of its aging 767s over the A330neos. Earlier, Hawaiian Air ( HA ) canceled an A330neo order and bought 787s instead, and American Airlines ( AAL ) also picked the 787 over the A350 and A330neo.
Blockchain, Artificial Intelligence Blockchain burst on the scene along with Bitcoin last year. While it was a buzzword at the 2017 Paris Air Show, John Schmidt, global managing director of aerospace and defense practices at Accenture, said this year's show will focus on what aerospace companies plan to do with the digital ledger technology.
Accenture said that 86% of aerospace industry planned to integrate blockchain into their systems within the next three years. The technology could be especially useful in preventing counterfeit parts, a major issue in the sector.
And as Apple 's ( AAPL ) Siri and Amazon 's ( AMZN ) Alexa transform life at home, the digital assistant concept is helping boost production amid workforce shortages.
"We are going to need to get more done with one person," Schmidt said. "AI is not replacing people but working next to them. Having a digital assistant on the assembly floor to remind workers 'when you're on this aircraft line, remember to do this.'"
